title: Context Platform Engineering to Reduce Token Anxiety — Val Bercovici, WEKA

summary: Val Bercovici and Callan Fox present context platform engineering as a discipline for designing, sizing, and configuring systems optimized for agent swarm context at any scale. They announce WEKA's open-source toolkit on GitHub, featuring a load generator that lets users configure agent swarms and subtasks with specific SLOs, cycling through deterministic and random prompt cycles, with model parallelism, disaggregated or aggregated pre-fill/decode, and memory tiering options. They frame the problem around token anxiety—rate limits and cost—and argue that without context platform engineering, users resort to context financial engineering, doing prompt arbitrage between input/output token pricing and cache read/write costs across TTLs like 5 minutes or 1 hour (Anthropic). A key insight is that subscribing to token tiers is effectively purchasing cache KV slots in token storage, and the platform must translate SLA requirements into SLOs. Fox visualizes the agent feedback loop: agents consume context to a high watermark, summarize, then restart—a cycle where summarization can reduce fidelity. Agentic coding prompts are mostly tool use and tool responses, not user input. Median time between requests is 10-15 seconds, but meantime is minutes to hours due to human response latency, creating a cadence mismatch. Multi-agent setups use orchestrators and sub-agents with shared common context. Real cache hit rates fall far below 100%, costing API users up to 10x more on misses and pushing subscription users toward rate limits faster. Temporal analysis shows 1-minute TTLs thrash when request gaps exceed the TTL, while 5-minute TTLs sustain more cache hits; 1-hour TTLs yield even better user and provider experiences but require holding significantly more tokens in cache. Fox also visualizes token refresh frequency—tokens re-prefilled 15-16 times at 1-minute TTL versus approaching 1 at higher TTLs. Shifting to the inference provider perspective (vision for 2026+), Fox shows the non-linear relationship between context length, cache hit rate, and output tokens, where providers must keep users in a high-hit-rate band or risk melting GPU clusters. Token storage needs sufficient capacity, extremely fast writes to avoid blocking GPUs, and rapid fetch. Memory tiers compared include HBM (ideal but impractical for all sessions), DRAM (common but size-limited and compute-coupled), pooled DRAM (limited benefit), and WEKA's NVMe-backed augmented memory grid (~1000x denser). Benchmark results comparing HBM+WEKA (purple), HBM+DRAM (orange), and HBM+DRAM+another storage system show all three leveraging HBM initially, but DRAM-based systems drop off dramatically as concurrent users increase. WEKA maintains higher concurrency and output tokens at steady state, with even better results in pre-fill-focused (disaggregated) configurations, because it combines cache capacity with DRAM-like speeds. Bercovici closes by encouraging downloads, feedback, and forks of the open-source toolkit.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Open-Source Toolkit Announcement
sections.summary: Val Bercovici and Callan Fox introduce themselves and announce WEKA's open-source context platform engineering toolkit on GitHub, featuring a load generator for agent swarm SLO configuration with model parallelism, pre-fill/decode options, and memory tiering.

sections.title: KV Cache Hit Rate and Token Anxiety
sections.summary: Cites Manus AI's claim that KV cache hit rate is the single most important metric for production AI agents. Introduces token anxiety from rate limits and positions context platform engineering as the systematic solution to maximize hit rates.

sections.title: Context Financial Engineering vs. Context Platform Engineering
sections.summary: Contrasts ad-hoc prompt arbitrage—balancing input/output token pricing against cache read/write costs across TTLs (5 min, 1 hr Anthropic)—with systematic context platform engineering. Highlights the cadence mismatch between slow human loops and fast agent iterations.

sections.title: SLA-to-SLO Translation and KV Slot Purchasing
sections.summary: Explains that token tier subscriptions are effectively purchasing cache KV slots in token storage, and context platform engineering translates agent SLA requirements into infrastructure SLOs by optimizing KV caching and memory tiers.

sections.title: Agent Token Consumption Visualization
sections.summary: Fox visualizes the agent loop as a column: agents consume context to a high watermark, summarize (losing fidelity), then restart. Agentic coding prompts are mostly tool use and tool responses. Median inter-request time is 10-15 seconds; meantime is minutes to hours due to human latency.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Context and Cache Miss Reality
sections.summary: Describes multi-agent orchestrator/sub-agent patterns with shared common context. Real cache hit rates fall well below 100%; API users pay up to 10x more on misses, subscription users hit rate limits faster.

sections.title: Temporal Working Set and TTL Impact on Hit Rate
sections.summary: Temporal analysis shows working set held in memory versus cache hit rate across TTLs. 1-minute TTL thrashes when request gaps exceed TTL; 5-minute TTL sustains more cache hits; 1-hour TTL yields better user and provider experiences but requires holding significantly more tokens. Token refresh visualization shows 15-16x re-prefills at 1-minute TTL approaching 1x at higher TTLs.

sections.title: Inference Provider Perspective and Cache Hit Rate Zones
sections.summary: Shifts to the inference provider perspective for 2026+. Shows a non-linear curve relating context length, cache hit rate, and output tokens, with providers needing to keep users in a high-hit-rate zone or risk melting GPU clusters. Reinforces that subscription tiers are effectively purchasing KV cache allocations.

sections.title: Token Storage Requirements and Memory Tier Comparison
sections.summary: Explains token storage needs: sufficient capacity for optimal cache, extremely fast writes to avoid blocking GPUs, and rapid fetch. Compares memory tiers: HBM (ideal but impractical for all sessions), DRAM (common but size-limited and compute-coupled), pooled DRAM (limited benefit), and WEKA's NVMe-backed augmented memory grid (~1000x denser).

sections.title: Testing Methodology: Static vs Increasing Users
sections.summary: Describes two testing approaches: deterministic sequential prompts that show sharp drop-off when memory tier overflows, and random sampling from a pool with increasing concurrent users for a blended benchmark. SLOs include time to first token and output tokens per request.

sections.title: Benchmark Results: Memory Tier Performance Comparison
sections.summary: Compares three configurations (HBM+WEKA purple, HBM+DRAM orange, HBM+DRAM+other pink). All leverage HBM initially; DRAM-based systems drop dramatically as users scale. WEKA maintains higher concurrency and output tokens at steady state. Disaggregated pre-fill yields even better results for WEKA due to GPU efficiency with large pre-fill batches.

sections.title: Closing and Call to Action
sections.summary: Bercovici closes by encouraging downloads, feedback, and forks of the open-source toolkit, emphasizing the goal of reducing token anxiety and prompt cache arbitrage through context platform engineering. Links to blogs and resources provided.
